Yes—my original claim was too sweeping, especially about employers’ motives. Remote work can offer flexibility and fewer interruptions, while working in person can help with mentoring, relationship-building, and some kinds of collaboration. Productivity outcomes vary by role, team, and how the arrangement is managed.

I’d rephrase it as: “Remote work has substantial benefits for many knowledge workers, but neither remote nor office-based work is universally better. The best approach depends on the work, individual needs, and team coordination—not simply a preference for control.”
